rounds.hypothesis: Per diagnose.json, two defects on one path: clock_getres is absent from both syscall dispatch tables (x86 229, generic 114), so it returns ENOSYS where the test expects 0 or EINVAL; and independently VdsoData.hrtimer_res is initialised to 0 and never written, so __vdso_clock_getres reports 0ns for the four high-resolution clocks. The invariant is that a clock's resolution is a property of the clock, identical no matter which path serves the request, so the resolution has to live on the clock itself (owning_layer) rather than being hardcoded in a new syscall handler.
rounds.change: Added `Clock::resolution()` to the trait in kernel/src/time/core/mod.rs with a `HIGH_RES_CLOCK_RESOLUTION` (1ns) default, plus a `TICK_CLOCK_RESOLUTION` constant derived from ostd's TIMER_FREQ. Overrode it on the tick-driven clocks: RealTimeCoarseClock/MonotonicCoarseClock and JiffiesClock in clocks/system_wide.rs, CpuClock/ProfClock in clocks/cpu_clock.rs. Factored the clockid_t-to-clock lookup out of read_clock() into a shared `with_clock()` helper in syscall/clock_gettime.rs (the analogue of Linux's clockid_to_kclock), so gettime and getres inherit one validation path. Added syscall/clock_getres.rs calling with_clock(), validating before the copy-out and skipping the write when res is NULL. Registered 229 (x86) and 114 (generic). Populated VdsoData.hrtimer_res in VdsoData::init() from MonotonicClock::get().resolution(), with debug_asserts that all four HIGH_RES_CLOCK_IDS agree. Uncommented clock_getres01 in all.txt.
rounds.outcome: green on the first round: `All conformance tests passed.`, make exit 0, kirk reports 36 passed / 0 failed / 0 broken / 8 skipped = 44 results, matching the host's 44 exactly. Verbose per-case output confirms all 4 variants ran (the 2 raw-syscall variants no longer abort with TCONF), that clockid -1 now yields EINVAL, and that the 8 skips are exactly the 2 unimplemented ALARM clocks x 4 variants recorded as TCONF. Because this test never inspects the resolution value it is handed, the values were verified separately (see below): a scratch checker booted in Asterinas showed 1ns from both the vDSO and the syscall for REALTIME/MONOTONIC/MONOTONIC_RAW/BOOTTIME -- the vDSO previously reported 0 -- and LTP's nanosleep01 independently printed 'CLOCK_MONOTONIC resolution 1ns' via the raw syscall.

layer: The POSIX clock abstraction in kernel/src/time, as diagnose.json's owning_layer specified. `Clock::resolution()` puts the value on the clock next to read_time(), and `with_clock()` makes the clockid_t-to-clock mapping a single shared point; the syscall handler and the vDSO data page are both consumers that read from there rather than deciding for themselves. Patching only the syscall (a hardcoded match on ClockId in clock_getres.rs) would have turned the test green while leaving the vDSO reporting 0ns for the same clocks -- green but self-inconsistent, which is exactly the failure mode this layer choice avoids.
generalizes: The rule is enforced where it is decided, so it holds for callers this test never exercises. (1) The vDSO was already wrong before this test existed: hrtimer_res = 0 meant every process on the system got 0ns from __vdso_clock_getres for CLOCK_REALTIME, CLOCK_MONOTONIC, CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW and CLOCK_BOOTTIME. That is fixed for all of them, not just the ones clock_getres01 asks about -- and clock_getres01 could not have caught it, since it never reads the value. Verified empirically with a scratch program (kept in /tmp, not committed) comparing the vDSO and raw-syscall answers for all 8 clocks: both now return 1ns for the high-res set and AGREE. (2) There is no branch anywhere on the specific clock ids, errnos, or the NULL-vs-non-NULL res that this test happens to supply. `with_clock` accepts every id read_clock accepts, so validity and EINVAL behaviour cannot diverge between gettime and getres by construction -- including the negative dynamic-clock encoding and the per-pid/per-tid clocks, which clock_getres01 never supplies but which now report a resolution correctly. (3) resolution() is defined for every Clock impl, so the CpuClock/ProfClock and JiffiesClock instances answer too, and any future consumer (e.g. clock_nanosleep rounding to timer granularity, which diagnose noted has nowhere to read this from today) gets one authoritative value. (4) Regression-checked the shared read_clock refactor across the whole enabled clock/timer surface -- clock_nanosleep01/04, getitimer01/02, setitimer02, timerfd01/02, timerfd_create01, timer_create03, timer_delete02, nanosleep01/02, gettimeofday02, time01, times01, futimesat01, utime07, epoll_wait04 -- 134 passed / 0 failed / 0 broken. One deliberate residual, documented in a FIXME in vdso.rs: the coarse clocks still disagree between paths (vDSO 4ms vs syscall 1ms) because the prebuilt Linux vDSO answers those from a constant compiled into the library (LOW_RES_NSEC) rather than from any VdsoData field, so there is no data-page field through which the kernel can correct it. That gap predates this change, is not reachable through the field I populated, and closing it requires Asterinas's own vDSO library.
fix_summary: Gives the clock layer a resolution and has all three consumers read it from there. Designed against Asterinas's `Clock` trait rather than transplanting Linux's structure: Linux carries a per-clock k_clock vtable with both .clock_get_timespec and .clock_getres, whereas Asterinas's Clock trait had only read_time() -- its doc comment already asserted a clock 'has a fixed resolution' while giving no way to obtain it, which was the actual gap. So `resolution()` became a defaulted trait method beside read_time() (default 1ns for clocks that read the clocksource, overridden to the tick period for the tick-driven ones), which is the Asterinas-shaped expression of Linux's per-clock .clock_getres hook. The clockid_t validation point is likewise expressed as a `with_clock(clockid, ctx, op)` helper that read_clock() is now a one-line wrapper over, playing the role of Linux's clockid_to_kclock() without introducing a vtable Asterinas does not otherwise have. Resolution values follow Linux: 1ns for the high-resolution clocks (Linux's hrtimer_resolution) and the tick period for the coarse ones (Linux's TICK_NSEC). One deliberate divergence, commented in cpu_clock.rs: Linux reports 1ns for CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID/CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID because there they map to CPUCLOCK_SCHED, backed by nanosecond-granular sched_clock, while it reports the tick period for its jiffies-based CPUCLOCK_PROF/VIRT. Asterinas's ProfClock accumulates whole jiffies via add_jiffies(), so it is the CPUCLOCK_PROF analogue and the tick period is the honest answer; reporting 1ns would be copying Linux's number while lacking the sched_clock that justifies it. The test accepts either, since it only checks the return value.
